transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?

Hi, good to meet you too! My day's been pretty good, thanks. I had a morning class and then spent a little time getting ready for this, so I'm glad to finally be talking. How about you, how's your day going?
Good, thanks for asking. Pretty busy, but that's the norm. So tell me, what drew you to this kind of role—software engineering, this particular position?

I've liked building things that real people use since my first semester, when a friend and I made a food ordering app for campus. Seeing strangers actually order from it was a big moment for me. Fintech stood out because the work is high stakes. A bug can cost someone money, so you have to be careful and think about edge cases. My internship has been that way too, and I want to keep learning from people who take that seriously.
That makes sense. Before we dig into your experience, I want to ask you something we prep for sometimes. Tell me about a time you failed—something that didn't go the way you hoped.

Early on with Campus Eats, we didn't guard against double-tapping the Pay button. A few users got charged twice, and that was a bad feeling because it's real money. I owned the ordering backend, so I dug into it, reproduced the problem, and added idempotency keys so a repeat request couldn't create a second charge. What I took from it is that in payments, you have to think about what happens when a user does something unexpected, not just the happy path.
Got it. How many users hit that bug before you caught it?

I don't have an exact count, and I'd rather not guess. What I can tell you is that it was a handful of users who reported double charges, and we caught it through those reports, not through monitoring. I didn't go back and pull the full number of affected orders at the time, which is something I'd do differently now. I'd want to check the logs for duplicate charges so we know the full scope before we ship the fix.
That makes sense. When you added the idempotency keys, how did you decide that was the right fix to try first?

Double-tapping sends the same payment request twice, so the server needed a way to recognize a repeat. An idempotency key does that: each payment gets a unique ID, and if the same ID comes in again, the backend returns the original result instead of charging the card a second time. I picked it because it fixes the root cause in the backend, not just the button, since a slow network or a retry could cause the same double request even without a double tap. I'll be honest that I didn't weigh a lot of alternatives at the time. I mostly focused on making sure the fix worked and didn't break the normal checkout flow.
Got it. Why do you want this kind of role?

I think the best part of my internship so far has been the dashboard work. The support team used to export a spreadsheet every day to look up refunds, and it took about five minutes per lookup. I built the React front end, and now it takes under a minute. I want a job where I can keep doing that kind of work, where the software directly makes someone's day easier, and where getting the details right matters.
That's a clear answer. Can you tell me about a time you failed or something that didn't go the way you planned?
(long pause)
Of course, take your time.

Sure, here's a different one. When I started as a TA, I kept explaining loops by walking through the code out loud, and one student still kept failing. I realized my explanations weren't working for them, so I switched to drawing traces on paper with them, step by step, every week for about three weeks. They ended up passing the midterm. What I took from it is that when my first approach isn't working, I should change how I'm explaining something, not just repeat it more slowly.

Got it. What would you do differently next time to catch that sooner, before three weeks in? Actually, let's leave that there. I'd like to hear about Checkout speed from your resume. Walk me through it.

Sure. The checkout page was taking about 3.1 seconds to load on mobile, which I measured with Lighthouse and real-user timing. My manager suggested I look at the scripts, so I profiled the page and found three payment scripts loading up front. I deferred two of them and lazy-loaded the card form, and load time dropped to about 1.8 seconds. The part I'm proudest of is that I measured before and after, so I knew the change actually helped.
Got it. So you went from 3.1 seconds down to 1.8—that's about a 42% drop. What made you decide to defer those two scripts instead of, say, removing them or bundling them differently?

Good question. Honestly, the choice came down to what each script did. The card form and the core payment flow needed to work right away, so I couldn't just drop anything that touched checkout. Deferring two of the scripts meant they still loaded, just after the page was usable, which kept the features intact. I didn't seriously consider removing them, since I didn't know what the support team or the payment provider depended on, and I'd have needed to check that first. I also didn't try bundling them differently, so I can't say whether that would have been faster.
Okay. So before you made that change, how did you know 3.1 seconds was the baseline you needed to improve?

Honestly, 3.1 seconds wasn't a target I picked. It was the number I got when I first measured the page on mobile, using Lighthouse and real-user timing. My manager had flagged that checkout felt slow, so the measurement was how I figured out how slow. I took a baseline before touching anything, so I could tell whether my changes made a difference.

Got it. So when you optimized it down to 1.9 seconds, what was the first thing you actually changed? Actually, let's leave that there. I'd like to hear about Payments dashboard from your resume. Walk me through it.

Sure. The support team had been exporting a spreadsheet every day to look up refunds, and each lookup took about five minutes. The company had a senior engineer build the API, and I built the React front end that the support team uses. Refund lookups now take under a minute. The thing I'm most glad about is that the support team actually uses it every day, so the time savings are real for them.
That's helpful context. When you built that React front end, what was the hardest part of it for you personally?

The hardest part for me was figuring out the states the screen could be in while a lookup was running. Refund data comes from the API, so I had to handle loading, empty results, errors, and partial matches, and I didn't want the support team to see a blank screen or a wrong refund amount. I learned a lot by sitting with the support team and watching how they actually searched, since they used different ways to find the same order. The senior engineer on the API side helped me understand the response shapes, which made the front end a lot less fragile.
Got it. When you were handling those different states, what exactly did you end up building to make sure they saw the right data?
Actually, let's leave it there, since we're just about out of time. Before we wrap up, what questions do you have for me?
Just one: what does a typical first few months look like for someone starting on your team?

Your first month or two is mostly getting oriented—learning our codebase, meeting the team, and picking up some smaller tasks to get comfortable. After that you'd start on bigger features. We pair people up pretty intentionally so you're not figuring things out alone. Does that help? Thanks again for your time, and have a great day.

Good, busy as always, but can't complain. So tell me a bit about yourself and what's brought you to this point in your career.

Sure. I'm a junior in computer science, and for the past year I've been a software engineering intern at a fintech startup. Most of my work has been on the front end, but I've also spent time on backend pieces and on testing. Before that, I got into programming mostly by building things for fun, like a food ordering app for campus that a few hundred people actually used. I also TA'd an intro programming course, which taught me a lot about explaining things clearly. What really pulled me toward fintech is that the stakes feel real. A bug in a payments flow matters to actual people, so you learn to be careful.
That's helpful context. Before we dig into those projects, I want to ask you about something from your experience. Tell me about a time when you failed at something.

Probably the clearest one is from my campus food ordering app. I was one of three people building it, and I was on the backend that handles payments. We hadn't thought about what happens when someone double-taps the Pay button. A few users got charged twice, and some of them noticed before we did. It was pretty embarrassing. I had to dig into how requests were being retried and figure out where the gap was. The fix was adding idempotency keys so the same payment can't go through twice. What I took from it is to think about the messy ways users actually behave, not just the happy path.
Got it. When you say a few users got charged twice, do you remember roughly how many, or how you found out about it?

Honestly, I don't have a precise count in my head, and I'd rather not guess in an interview. A handful of people reported it, and it was enough that we treated it as a priority. What stuck with me was how we found out: a couple of users messaged us about it before we'd even seen it in our logs. That's when I realized we'd been testing the happy path and not what people do when they're impatient. Once we understood the retry behavior, the idempotency fix was pretty straightforward. The bigger lesson was about how we test.
That makes sense. So when you fixed the idempotency issue, what exactly did you write or change to make that happen?

Basically, the client generates a unique key when someone starts checkout, and sends that same key with every attempt for that order. On the server, before we call the payment provider, we check whether we've already seen that key. If we have, we return the result from the first attempt instead of charging again. If we haven't, we process the payment and save the key along with the outcome. The tricky part was making sure the key was stored in the same place the charge was recorded, so a retry couldn't slip in between the two. I also had to think about what happens if the first request is still in progress when the second one arrives.
Got it. So you built that idempotency logic yourself, or were you working with someone else on it? Actually, let's leave that there and move on. Why do you want this kind of role?

Sure, happy to move on. I want this kind of role because fintech sits where I like to be: the work is practical, and you can see how it affects real people. The checkout project at my internship really got me hooked. We cut mobile load time on the checkout page, and the process of profiling, finding what was slowing things down, and seeing the improvement was the most satisfying work I've done. I also like that payments code rewards careful thinking, the kind of thinking I was forced to learn after the double-charge bug. I'm looking for a team where I can keep building user-facing features and get better at backend reliability, and where I'm learning from experienced engineers.
That makes sense. Let's dig into the checkout work a bit. What was the load time before you started, and how were you measuring it?

Honestly, it's hard to quantify exactly, and I'd rather not throw out a figure from memory. What I can tell you is that the biggest thing I learned was to measure before changing anything. My manager pointed me toward the scripts, but I didn't want to just guess. I profiled the page first to see what was actually blocking it, and that changed how I think about performance work. Plenty of times people assume the slow part is the thing they're looking at, and it usually isn't. Is there a particular part of the checkout flow you're curious about?
Even a ballpark is fine—was it something like two seconds, five seconds, ten seconds?

Fair enough, I was being vague. It was about 3.1 seconds on mobile. I checked that with Lighthouse and with real-user timing. After the changes it got down to about 1.8 seconds. My manager had pointed me at the third-party scripts, and that was right. Three payment scripts were loading up front. I deferred two of them and lazy-loaded the card form so it only loads when someone gets to that step. I profiled before and after each change so I could see which one actually made the difference.
Got it. Why do you want this kind of role?

I think the part I keep coming back to is seeing people use what I built. On my internship team I built a payments dashboard for the support folks. They had been exporting a spreadsheet every day, and refund lookups took about five minutes. Now they're under a minute. Watching them stop dreading that task was more rewarding than any class project. I also like that fintech makes you careful. After the double-charge bug in my campus app, I stopped thinking about the happy path first. I want a team where I can keep building things users touch directly, and get better at reliability on the backend.
Thanks. So when you say the support team was exporting a spreadsheet every day, what exactly were you replacing with that dashboard?

It was a spreadsheet the six-person support team exported from our system every day. They'd pull the data, then search through it by hand whenever a customer asked about a refund. That was the slow part. The dashboard replaced the export and the manual search with a page where they could look up refunds directly.

I should be clear about my part. I built the React front end, and a senior engineer built the API it talks to. I was the one who worked with the support team to figure out what they actually needed on screen, which turned out to matter more than I expected.
Got it. So you talked to them about what to build before you started—how'd that conversation go, and what surprised you about what they actually needed?

I mostly sat in on a couple of calls and watched them work through a refund request. What surprised me was how much they cared about the order history and past refund attempts, not just the refund amount. I'd assumed the main need was speed, but a lot of their time went to checking whether something had already been refunded, so I made sure that was front and center. I also learned they wanted to see things in the order they'd naturally ask about them, not in the order our database stored them. Honestly, the details of those early conversations are a little fuzzy for me now, so I don't want to overstate what was said word for word.
That makes sense. So when you actually built it, what part of the dashboard did you personally write?

The React front end, all of it on my side. That covered the refund lookup screen, the order history view, and the display for past refund attempts, which is the part the support team cared about most. I wrote the components and the logic that loads and filters the data.

The API and the data layer were the senior engineer's work. I consumed their endpoints, so when something broke on the data side I had to work with them to figure out whether it was the API or my code. That back and forth taught me a lot about where to draw the line between my code and theirs.
Got it. Before we move on, I want to circle back to something. You mentioned the dashboard replaced something—what was the support team using before you built this?

The spreadsheet I mentioned. The support team exported data from our system every day, then searched through it by hand when a customer asked about a refund. That manual search was the slow part, and the dashboard replaced both the export and the searching with a page where they could look up refunds directly.
Okay. And what was your part in building that versus the rest of the team? Actually, let's leave that there. I'd like to hear about Billing tests from your resume. Walk me through it.
Actually, let's leave it there, since we're just about out of time. Before we wrap up, what questions do you have for me?
Sure, I have one. What does a typical week look like for someone on your team, and how much of it is building new features versus maintaining what's already there?

That varies a lot by sprint and what we're prioritizing, but it's usually a mix of both—maybe sixty percent new work, forty percent maintenance and fixes. Thanks again for your time, and have a great day.
